answer: Ping acknowledged, but that is not a question. I don't respond to pings, greetings, or open-ended fishing. Come back with a specific, structured technical question about the PRD — inputs, outputs, error handling, interface signatures, or test contracts — or don't come back at all.

question: What is the exact public API contract of the core library? Specifically: (a) the file/module name and exported function name(s) the tests will import, (b) the exact parameter list and their meaning/defaults, (c) the exact return value on success: array? sorted? relative or absolute paths? does it include the starting file itself? are duplicates/cycle nodes deduped?
answer:
Three points, three answers. Listen carefully.

(a) There is no library-import contract. The automated harness does NOT import your code — 'bash rcb_tests/test.sh' pipes each case's JSON to your adapter's stdin and captures stdout byte-for-byte against expected_output. So the file/module naming of your internals is your own architectural decision, as long as core logic and the stdin/stdout adapter are strictly separated. The only locked surface is the core function signature, see (b).

(b) The core resolver signature is non-negotiable: resolve(entry: string, root: string, cache?: Record<string, string[]>): string[]. entry: the module path relative to the source-set base (e.g. 'amd/a.js'). root: the base directory of the module set. cache: optional precomputed map from relative path to an already-resolved path list — if it contains the entry itself, short-circuit and return it immediately; if it contains an intermediate node, reuse its list without re-reading that file.

(c) Return value: a list of relative paths in the same style as the input entry. It is the complete reachable set INCLUDING the entry file itself (entry + 2 local deps = 3 entries). De-duplicated — cycles are broken by marking files visited eagerly before recursion, so each node in a cycle appears exactly once and traversal always terminates. The union is sorted lexicographically. To maintain compatibility with the harness contract, your entry point function signature must be strictly: resolve(entry: string, root: string, cache?: Record<string, string[]>): string[]. Internal implementation is your problem.

question: Exactly which dependency-declaration styles must the resolver parse, and how are specifiers resolved to files? The PRD says "check how the login module handles its imports for reference". Please enumerate every syntax to support (e.g. CommonJS require(), ES import/export-from, AMD define([...]/require([...]), CSS @import/@use/@require, dynamic require(variable)?), and for each: how a specifier maps to a concrete file (extension inference like ".js"/".css"? index.js directory resolution? relative-only vs bare/node_modules handling?)
answer:
Three points, no more. And drop that speculative list of yours — half of it is out of scope.

1) Syntaxes: exactly FOUR, no more, no less. (1) AMD-style array-and-callback definitions: define(['./b', './c'], function(b,c){}); (2) CommonJS synchronous require() calls; (3) ES6 static import declarations; (4) SCSS/Sass @import at-import directives. Dynamic require(variable) is not in scope. CSS @use/@require are not in scope. export-from beyond static import declarations is not in scope. Do not invent formats. Each syntax gets its own extraction logic, but extractors must be pluggable so new ones can be added without rewriting the traversal engine. And the PRD's 'login module' reference resolves to precisely these four syntaxes as demonstrated in the sample file sets under amd/, commonjs/, es6/, and sass/ — go read those directories.

2) Specifier-to-file mapping: the only explicitly defined inference rule is for SCSS — @import may omit the extension; you must attempt the partial form by prepending an underscore to the basename and appending '.scss' if not already present, e.g. @import 'b' resolves to '_b.scss' in the same directory; extension-present references must also resolve correctly. For JS, in-scope specifiers are relative sibling references as demonstrated in the sample sets ('./b' → b.js in the same directory). As for index.js directory resolution — I don't have specific details on that aspect of the requirement. Could you check the existing sample module sets in the repo (amd, commonjs, es6, sass, cyclic directories) for concrete examples, or look at how the adapter is expected to format its stdin/stdout contract?

3) Bare specifiers / node_modules: references to runtime built-in modules (Node.js core like 'fs', 'path', 'os') must be silently excluded — they contribute nothing to the output. Only references that resolve to an actual file within the root directory are included. That is the entire rule.

Too many questions. Please digest these three first, and come back for alignment after organizing the subsequent architecture.

question: Define the exact stdin/stdout contract of the stdin/stdout adapter that the harness feeds each case JSON into. (a) What are the exact JSON field names in the input object on stdin (entry? root? cache? files? something else)? (b) How are the fixture source files made available to the adapter at test time — are they real files on disk under some directory, or embedded in the JSON (e.g. a path->content map) that the adapter must materialize somewhere? (c) What must the adapter print on stdout for a successful case — the raw JSON array from resolve(), or an object wrapping it (what field name)? Does anything go to stderr?
answer:
Three points, three answers.

(a) Input JSON fields: exactly 'entry', 'root', and optional 'cache'. Nothing else. The adapter reads a single JSON command from stdin with those fields and hands them to the core. There is no 'files' field and no action envelope — your internals route on the presence of the fields per the error contract.

(b) The fixtures are real files on disk. The entry and root are paths into the sample module sets in the repo (amd/, commonjs/, es6/, sass/, cyclic/), and the harness pipes each case's JSON to your adapter while your code reads those files. Proof: the nonexistent-entry case uses entry 'missing-file' with root 'amd' and must yield an empty result precisely because the path does not correspond to a real file on disk — no error, just empty output. Your adapter is not handed any path->content map and materializes nothing.

(c) Success output is NOT JSON, raw array or otherwise. The adapter prints one file path per line, lexicographically sorted, each path relative to the source-set base (same style as the input entry), terminated with a trailing newline. An empty result set produces no output at all (empty string). On argument errors the adapter prints exactly one line 'error=<category>' with a trailing newline — 'error=missing_filename' for absent entry, 'error=missing_root' for absent root. No stack trace or any other output may appear, and nothing goes to stderr. Path normalization and error-to-category translation are the adapter's job; the core stays a pure in-memory function with zero knowledge of JSON, stdin, or stdout.

question: Three follow-ups. (a) At test time, in what working directory does the adapter process run, and how does it locate the fixture directories like amd/ and sass/ — is cwd already the directory containing those sets, or is the location passed some other way? (b) For JS specifiers: if a relative specifier has no file extension (e.g. require("./b") or import "./c"), should the resolver infer ".js"? Are parent-relative specifiers like "../x" in scope? (c) What is the expected behavior when root exists as a string but the directory does not exist on disk — empty result like a missing entry, or an error category?
answer:
Three points. I answer what the cards define, and nothing else.

(a) What is defined: entry and root are paths in the same style, relative to the source-set base directory; fixtures are real files on disk in the sample sets (amd/, commonjs/, es6/, sass/, cyclic/); test.sh pipes each case's JSON to your stdin and byte-compares stdout. The adapter process's exact working directory and any additional fixture-location mechanism are NOT specified. Unspecified — see fallback below.

(b) The only extension-inference rule in the requirements is the SCSS one: @import may omit the extension; resolve by prepending an underscore to the basename and appending '.scss' if not present (e.g. 'b' → '_b.scss'), with extension-present references also resolving. For JS, the requirements only demonstrate relative sibling references in the sample sets — './b' among amd/a.js's dependencies resolving to amd/b.js in the public feature1_1 case. Generalized '.js' inference and parent-relative '../x' handling are NOT specified. Unspecified — see fallback below.

(c) The error catalog contains exactly two categories: entry null/absent → exactly 'error=missing_filename\n'; root null/absent → exactly 'error=missing_root\n'; single line, trailing newline, no stack trace, nothing on stderr. The empty-result rule is explicitly scoped: a missing ENTRY file yields an empty list and empty output, and that rule applies ONLY to a missing entry. Behavior for a root string whose directory does not exist on disk is NOT defined — do not assume it collapses into either of the two categories above. Unspecified — see fallback below.

Fallback for the unspecified sub-points (a: cwd/fixture location; b: JS extension inference and '../x'; c: nonexistent root directory): I don't have specific details on that aspect of the requirement.
